AML-STC. The AML-STC must comply with the requirements of 14 CFR part 21,\nsubpart E, for the issuance of STCs.\na. The applicability of the baseline data for each model must clearly be established.\nb. An AML-STC is issued for aircraft that are type-certificated in the same category (e.g., an \nAML-STC for an aircraft certificated under 14 CFR part 23 cannot include aircraft certificated \nunder parts 25, 27, or 29. Further, it is recommended that each category of aircraft within 14 CFR \npart 23 (i.e., normal, utility, acrobatic, and commuter) have a separate AML-STC due to possible \ndifferences that may exist in the certification requirements. This depends on the type of \nmodification to the affected area (e.g. structure, powerplant, systems, avionics, etc.).\nCoordination with the responsible ACO may be required to review the proposed modification and \ndetermine whether it is necessary to issue a separate AML-STC to document the specific \ncertification requirement for each category.\nc. Compliance with the requirements of section 21.20 and applicable data must be shown for \nevery model on the AML (e.g., type design, substantiating data, and flight manual supplement\n(FMS)). Whether this data is generated from testing (e.g., flight testing), or re-submitted from a\nprevious approval, substantiation for each additional aircraft model is required. When adding new \nmodel(s) or amending an existing model, an AML-STC approval allows the use of previouslysubmitted compliance data that are applicable without the need for further review. If adding a new\nmodel that has differences from the previously-approved models, then further substantiation may\nbe required in order to address those differences. The AML-STC is not meant to be a blanket \napproval by allowing additional models without further substantiation.\nd. The certification basis and amendment level to the areas affected by the modification is \nestablished for each model.\ne. The modification to the affected area does not create an acoustical change to the typecertificated product per section 21.93(b).\nf. The Flight Manual Supplement (FMS) is applicable to each model per section 21.5.\ng. The AML-STC may not be suitable for systems that can directly control the aircraft. For\nexample, autopilot installations or similar systems that involve control inputs may require careful \ndesign installation, and testing on each proposed model regardless of baseline data shared between \nthem. For these types of installations, there may be serial number specific requirements that have\nto be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Another example would be an STC for reduced vertical \nseparation minimum (RVSM) equipment, where the model and serial number specific static\nsource error correction curve for RVSM approval is only applicable to a single serial number\naircraft.\nh. It is important for those who are seeking an AML-STC approval to discuss their plan early\nwith their respective aircraft certification office (ACO). AML-STC. The AML-STC must comply with the requirements of 14 CFR part 21,\nsubpart E, for the issuance of STCs.\na. The applicability of the baseline data for each model must clearly be established.\nb. An AML-STC is issued for aircraft that are type-certificated in the same category (e.g., an \nAML-STC for an aircraft certificated under 14 CFR part 23 cannot include aircraft certificated \nunder parts 25, 27, or 29. Further, it is recommended that each category of aircraft within 14 CFR \npart 23 (i.e., normal, utility, acrobatic, and commuter) have a separate AML-STC due to possible \ndifferences that may exist in the certification requirements. This depends on the type of \nmodification to the affected area (e.g. structure, powerplant, systems, avionics, etc.).\nCoordination with the responsible ACO may be required to review the proposed modification and \ndetermine whether it is necessary to issue a separate AML-STC to document the specific \ncertification requirement for each category.\nc. Compliance with the requirements of section 21.20 and applicable data must be shown for \nevery model on the AML (e.g., type design, substantiating data, and flight manual supplement\n(FMS)). Whether this data is generated from testing (e.g., flight testing), or re-submitted from a\nprevious approval, substantiation for each additional aircraft model is required. When adding new \nmodel(s) or amending an existing model, an AML-STC approval allows the use of previouslysubmitted compliance data that are applicable without the need for further review. If adding a new\nmodel that has differences from the previously-approved models, then further substantiation may\nbe required in order to address those differences. The AML-STC is not meant to be a blanket \napproval by allowing additional models without further substantiation.\nd. The certification basis and amendment level to the areas affected by the modification is \nestablished for each model.\ne. The modification to the affected area does not create an acoustical change to the typecertificated product per section 21.93(b).\nf. The Flight Manual Supplement (FMS) is applicable to each model per section 21.5.\ng. The AML-STC may not be suitable for systems that can directly control the aircraft. For\nexample, autopilot installations or similar systems that involve control inputs may require careful \ndesign installation, and testing on each proposed model regardless of baseline data shared between \nthem. Maintenance Procedures.\nShop procedures must follow the lithium battery manufacturer’s recommendations.\n3.1.8 Aircraft Battery Inspection.\nEvidence of battery failure can sometimes be detected by a visual inspection.\nManufacturer-recommended inspections should include, but not be limited to, the \nfollowing actions:\n3.1.8.1 Inspect battery terminals and all other connections for evidence of \ncorrosion, pitting, arcing, and burns. Clean as required.\n3.1.8.2 Inspect the battery for improper installation (loose terminal screws, battery \nterminal links, or connector).\n3.1.8.3 Inspect the battery mounting.\n3.1.8.4 Inspect for evidence of physical damage including heat \ndamage/discoloration.\n3.1.9 Batteries in a rotating stock must be functionally checked at the manufacturer’s \nrecommended inspection intervals. Some failure modes may include degraded charge \nretention capability, settling of particulates, or other damage due to prolonged storage.\nBatteries in rotating stock may also require periodic servicing per the manufacturer’s \ninstructions.\n3.2 Aircraft Battery Replacement.\n3.2.1 Make sure replacement batteries are in airworthy condition. Refer to the battery \nmanufacturer maintenance manuals for proper maintenance of lithium batteries. Refer \nto the aircraft maintenance procedures for replacement of lithium batteries.\n3.2.2 The ICA should include the manufacturer’s recommendations for the battery mandatory\nreplacement schedule and periodic maintenance.\n\n3-3\n3.2.3 Installation of lithium batteries differs from aircraft system to aircraft system. Refer to \nthe applicable aircraft manuals to remove and install batteries.\n3.2.4 When replacing batteries, check for corrosion and moisture on the battery interfaces.\n3.2.5 When replacing batteries, check for short circuit to battery case such as insulation \nresistance test.\n3.2.6 The maintenance record should reflect all battery replacements.
